```{r setup, include=FALSE}
is_cran_check <- !isTRUE(as.logical(Sys.getenv("NOT_CRAN", "false")))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svglite" else "png",
  fig.ext = if (requireNamespace("svglite", quietly = TRUE)) "svg" else "png",eval = !is_cran_check, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

An assessment team wants to discuss a difference in severity between two
raters. The point estimate answers how large the fitted difference is. Its
interval describes uncertainty under specified sampling and model assumptions.
Neither a difference nor an interval excluding zero establishes that a rater
is scoring incorrectly.

This guide first compares two covariance methods for **the same fitted estimates**.
The ordinary method uses the fitted model's observed information. The sandwich
method also uses the variation in likelihood contributions between independent
persons, or between explicitly declared larger clusters. It can change interval
widths without correcting biased estimates. It then introduces CML, which changes
the estimator by conditioning out Person parameters, and distinguishes native
contrasts from contrasts standardized by a fitted population SD. The examples
use fictional ratings.

## Fit the model and identify the comparison

```{r fit}
library(mfrmr)
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
fit <- fit_mfrm(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
                model = "RSM", method = "MML")
ordinary <- mfrm_facet_intervals(fit, "Rater")
summary(ordinary)
```

These are RSM marginal maximum likelihood estimates with a fixed standard-normal
person distribution. The interval helper also supports PCM in this scope, with
unit observation weights and fixed quadrature. It checks the source fit's
inference readiness. When an eligible fit has unavailable, nonpositive or
regularized joint information, the returned table retains finite points with
`Status = "information_unavailable"`, `CIEligible = FALSE` and missing
uncertainty. `InferenceReview` explains the failure, including any information
memory limit. Both model and sandwich intervals need the inverse information,
so switching to sandwich does not resolve this failure. Weak information can
also limit confidence in the point's numerical accuracy. Constraint-fixed
targets retain zero SE and no inferential interval. Invalid inputs and
ineligible source fits still produce errors.
For `method = "model"`, RSM/PCM singleton-category fits can pass a separate
review of the actual joint information, convergence and finer quadrature while
retaining `InferenceReady = FALSE` in the source fit. Read the interval object's
`CIEligible`, `checks` and `InferenceCaution`. This supplies an asymptotic
approximation with a small-sample caution; it does not establish coverage or
make other analyses available. Empty categories in a fitted step scope and identification/numerical
failures are not waived. To distinguish an unused rubric category from a
constant rater or criterion, supply the original score limits and
`category_policy = "preserve"` to `describe_mfrm_data()`. Compare
`score_distribution` with `MinScore` and `MaxScore` in `facet_level_summary`.
For an unused middle category within one rater, inspect the full count table,
here `table(ratings$Rater, factor(ratings$Score, levels = 1:4))`.
A local rater need not use every category of a shared step ladder when
full-information and quadrature checks pass. There is no ten-rating-row minimum; precision and
identification depend on the model and response patterns, not a row count alone.

Full RSM/PCM calibration also admits one Person for JML, CML and fixed-population
MML when the applicable checks pass. A single Person with informative independent
rating events can have finite structural estimates. This does not establish
small-sample coverage: returned interval tables retain `CoverageQualified = FALSE`
and a single-Person `InferenceCaution`. One Person cannot provide independent-
Person sandwich uncertainty or empirical between-Person variation. JML remains
a point-estimation route. Repeated ratings need a justified independence
declaration; duplicating records or relabeling ratings as Persons is not a remedy.

The default output lists each rater. With the default sum-to-zero constraint,
zero is the fitted reference across these raters; a positive value means more severe
ratings. To compare R01 with R02, request their **difference**. Subtracting two
estimates requires their covariance. Looking for overlap between their separate
intervals does not calculate an interval for that difference.

```{r contrast}
contrast <- matrix(c(1, -1, 0, 0), nrow = 1,
  dimnames = list("R01 minus R02", c("R01", "R02", "R03", "R04")))
difference <- mfrm_facet_intervals(fit, "Rater", contrasts = contrast,
                                  method = "sandwich")
summary(difference)
```

Positive values mean that R01 is more severe than R02 on this fitted scale, in
logits. The named coefficients also support other prespecified linear
comparisons. All facet levels must appear as columns, including those with
zero coefficients. Columns are matched by name.

`Estimate` is common to both methods. `SE`, `Lower` and `Upper` describe the
selected method; `ModelSE`, `ModelLower` and `ModelUpper` retain the ordinary
comparison. `Status` reports whether the selected interval is available.
These are pointwise normal intervals, not simultaneous protection for a set of
comparisons. Choosing whichever method gives a preferred conclusion is not a
valid analysis strategy.

```{r contrast-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="The same estimated rater contrast with model-based and one-way Person-sandwich normal intervals, offset vertically for comparison. Zero denotes no contrast, not a practical-importance or rater-quality threshold."}
plot(difference)
```

The slight vertical offset distinguishes the methods. Both points have the
same horizontal coordinate. The zero line denotes no difference; it is not a
threshold of practical importance or a rater-quality rule. Use the size of the
difference, interval, rubric and shared rating examples together when giving
feedback.

### Compare two scoring panels on shared essays

Suppose R01 and R02 form panel A and R03 and R04 form panel B. Each person
contributes one essay. Count essays scored by both panels before interpreting
their mean severity difference. An essay scored twice within A links two
raters but contributes no direct comparison with B.

```{r two-scoring-panels}
panel <- c(R01 = "A", R02 = "A", R03 = "B", R04 = "B")
assigned <- ratings
assigned$Panel <- unname(panel[as.character(assigned$Rater)])
stopifnot(!anyNA(assigned$Panel))
design <- describe_mfrm_data(assigned, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion", "Panel"),
                            "Score", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4, include_agreement = FALSE)
subset(design$linkage_summary, Facet %in% c("Rater", "Panel"),
       select = c(Facet, Persons, LinkingPersons))

weights <- matrix(c(-.5, -.5, .5, .5), nrow = 1,
                  dimnames = list("Panel B minus A", names(panel)))
panel_ci <- mfrm_facet_intervals(fit, "Rater", contrasts = weights)
panel_ci$table[, c("Target", "Estimate", "SE", "Lower", "Upper", "CIEligible", "InferenceReview")]
```

Read `LinkingPersons` on the `Panel` row for the shared count. With zero
shared essays, separating panel severity from differences between writer
cohorts requires another justified link or population assumption. With one
shared essay, all direct between-panel evidence comes from that essay. For
repeated performances, count the same work rated by both panels using its
performance ID.

Panel membership is used here to describe assignments. The fitted model
already estimates each rater's severity. For unequal panel sizes, give each
member of A weight `-1/n_A` and each member of B weight `+1/n_B`.
The reported SE uses the full rater covariance matrix. Report the shared
essay count, interval width and eligibility together.

## Compare raters when their criterion effects differ

A prespecified Rater × Criterion interaction allows a rater to be relatively
severe on one criterion and lenient on another. The rater main effect then
describes severity **averaged equally over the declared criteria**. It does not
weight criteria by their observed counts or estimate a difference in mean ratings.
Opposite departures on two criteria can leave a rater's overall Infit inside
the review band. For a prespecified concern, inspect the counts and observed
minus expected scores in `estimate_bias(fit, diagnose_mfrm(fit), "Rater", "Criterion")$table`
alongside the original ratings.

<details>
<summary>Fit the joint model and obtain the rater main-effect interval</summary>

```{r joint-main-effects, eval=FALSE}
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
persons <- unique(ratings["Person"])
joint_fit <- fit_mfrm(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  model = "RSM",
  spec = list(facet_interactions = "Rater:Criterion", population_formula = ~1,
              person_data = persons),
  control = list(mml_engine = "direct", quad_points = 121, maxit = 400,
                 reltol = 1e-11))
C <- matrix(c(1, -1, 0, 0), nrow = 1,
  dimnames = list("R01 minus R02", c("R01", "R02", "R03", "R04")))
main_interval <- mfrm_facet_intervals(joint_fit, facet = "Rater", contrasts = C)
main_interval$table
main_interval$checks
plot(main_interval, comparison = FALSE)
results <- mfrm_results(joint_fit, intervals = list(rater = main_interval),
                       compute = "never")
saveRDS(results, "joint-rater-results.rds")
mfrm_report(readRDS("joint-rater-results.rds"))
```

`persons` supplies one row per Person for the estimated population model.
This longer calibration is explicit code to run locally. For criterion-owned
steps, use `model = "PCM", step_facet = "Criterion"` in the same call.

</details>

Omitting `contrasts` returns every rater level, including the dependent last
level with its uncertainty. The interval uses the full joint covariance,
including estimation of interaction effects, steps and the ability population.
Only the model-information method on the native scale is supported here, with
one fitted interaction and the same source and numerical checks as joint-cell
intervals. Read `Status`, `CIEligible` and `InferenceReview`; withheld SE and
bounds remain missing even when the point is finite. Numerical availability
does not guarantee small-sample coverage.

To inspect the interaction itself, use
`mfrm_facet_intervals(joint_fit, interaction = "Rater:Criterion")`.
Its positive coefficients increase the score predictor. At criterion c, the
rater severity difference is `(r1 - r2) - (gamma1c - gamma2c)`; averaging this
equally over criteria gives the main-effect difference because interaction
margins sum to zero. Criterion-specific or unequal-weighted combined intervals
are outside the main-effect route. Neither result alone establishes unfairness.

## Estimate a rater difference without an ability population model

Suppose the target is a fixed rater-severity difference, and a normal ability
population would be a questionable assumption. For RSM/PCM, conditional maximum
likelihood (CML) conditions on each person's total across their observed ratings.
The ability parameter then cancels from the likelihood. This changes the
estimator, so its estimates need not equal the MML estimates above.

```{r cml-contrast}
if (requireNamespace("lpSolve", quietly = TRUE)) {
  cml_ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
  cml_fit <- fit_mfrm(cml_ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
    method = "CML", model = "RSM", rating_min = 1, rating_max = 4,
    category_policy = "preserve")
  cml_contrast <- matrix(c(1, -1, 0, 0), nrow = 1,
    dimnames = list("R01 minus R02", c("R01", "R02", "R03", "R04")))
  cml_interval <- mfrm_facet_intervals(cml_fit, "Rater", cml_contrast)
  print(summary(cml_interval))
  print(summary(cml_fit)$steps)
  cml_fit$checks
}
```

The comparison's `Estimate`, `SE`, `Lower` and `Upper` answer the same native-scale
rater-difference question. Its covariance comes from the **full conditional
information**, including jointly estimated criterion effects and steps.
`summary(cml_fit)$locations` lists the centered facet estimates. Use
`model = "PCM", step_facet = "Criterion"` when criteria own separate steps.
The package computes conditional normalizing constants with a generalized ESF
recursion and checks identification, finite-MLE existence and numerical convergence.
The optional `lpSolve` package is needed for the finite-MLE check.

If those checks pass but conditional information cannot be evaluated or safely
inverted, the fit retains its finite numerical point estimates with a warning.
Read `cml_fit$checks$information_status` and
`cml_fit$checks$information_reason`. Summaries and facet intervals keep the
points, with missing SE/bounds, `CIEligible = FALSE` and a reason in
`InferenceReview`; `vcov()` returns an `NA` matrix and default `confint()`
retains missing bounds with diagnostic reasons. A small score residual alone
does not ensure point accuracy along weak directions. Retention allows the
result to be inspected and saved; it does not qualify formal inference.
Identification, boundary and stationarity failures remain separate restrictions.

```{r cml-contrast-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="A CML estimate of the R01 minus R02 severity contrast with a pointwise 95 percent conditional-information Wald interval on the native logit scale."}
if (requireNamespace("lpSolve", quietly = TRUE)) plot(cml_interval, comparison = FALSE)
```

Save `cml_fit` and `cml_interval` with `saveRDS()` to retain the covariance,
contrast and checks. The dedicated `mfrm_cml_fit` has no Person estimates or
population distribution. Ordinary fit diagnostics and consolidated
`mfrm_results()` reports are outside this initial route; the interval object's
own summary and plot are available.

CML can remain consistent when the number of Persons grows with a fixed number
of ratings per Person, under a correct conditional response model, independent
Persons, fixed structural dimension and information growing in every identified
direction. Adding only extreme-total Persons does not improve precision, and
a contrast supported by only a few Persons can remain imprecise even in a large
dataset. The conditional model must hold for the actual rating roster;
response-dependent assignment, stopping or missingness needs separate justification.
This does not guarantee nominal Wald coverage in a small sample. See
`help("fit_mfrm")` for a sufficient regular regime and the covariance calculation
for an identified subspace. A facet constant within
each Person, such as school membership, disappears on conditioning: its main
effect cannot be estimated by CML. The full-model route refuses a deficient
parameterization. For identifiable interaction contrasts despite other aliased
directions, use the explicit `fit_scope = "comparisons"` route demonstrated in
[mfrmr Linking and DFF](https://ryuya-dot-com.github.io/mfrmr/dev/articles/mfrmr-linking-and-dff.html); unavailable targets remain missing.

A bounded check reused the earlier MML comparison's data-generation settings and
seeds: RSM/PCM, 80/320 Persons, and either six ratings under a normal ability
distribution or three ratings under a standardized-lognormal ability distribution
with two sparse rosters. All 1,600 CML fits returned the four prespecified native
contrasts. In the combined skewed/sparse conditions, truth coverage was
93.0–98.0%, compared with the earlier MML sandwich range of 87.0–95.5% on the
same datasets. Across all conditions CML coverage ranged from 92.5 to 98.5%.
Each condition has 200 replications, giving MCSE about 1.54 percentage points
near 95%. These ranges describe particular conditions and dependent contrasts;
they do not establish nominal coverage for every design. Because population
shape and roster sparsity changed together, this comparison does not isolate
their separate effects.

## Standardize by the same fit's estimated ability SD

For an MML fit with `population_formula = ~1`,
`mfrm_facet_intervals(fit, "Rater", contrasts = contrast, scale = "standardized")`
divides the contrast by that fit's estimated ability population SD. The contrast
must have coefficients summing to zero. It uses the joint delta method, including
the covariance between the contrast and the estimated SD; simply dividing an
existing interval by the fitted SD omits that uncertainty.

If the native contrast is \(\delta\), \(\lambda=\log\sigma^2\), and
\(d=\delta\exp(-\lambda/2)\), its derivative with respect to
\((\delta,\lambda)\) is \((1/\sigma,-d/2)\). The full fitted covariance is
transformed by this derivative:

\[
\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat d)=
\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat\delta)
+\widehat\delta^2\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}(\widehat\lambda)/4
-\widehat\delta\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\widehat\delta,\widehat\lambda)}
{\widehat\sigma^2}.
\]

Because of the covariance term, accounting for estimated SD does not always
increase the SE. Even a zero estimated contrast can have positive uncertainty.
This is an effect-size contrast, not the
Wald statistic obtained by dividing by the contrast's SE.

The regular delta method requires a fixed true SD strictly above zero and a
correctly specified, identified marginal model with an interior solution and
sufficient information. A positive fitted SD alone does not establish these
conditions. At zero SD the target is undefined; near zero the ratio and its
normal approximation can be unstable. There is no universal SD cutoff that
certifies validity. Population assumptions must hold for the actual rating
assignments and covariates; an overall normal distribution need not remain the
same within rosters selected according to ability.

MML also approximates a continuous integral. A fixed number of integration
points can leave numerical error as the sample grows and sampling SEs shrink.
Comparing quadrature orders is a useful sensitivity check, but agreement does
not prove that numerical error is negligible. Standardization repairs neither
integration error nor a misspecified ability distribution. See the MML
assumptions in `?mfrm_facet_intervals` before interpreting these normal intervals.

CML estimates no population SD, so this particular standardized contrast is
unavailable from a CML fit alone. A standard deviation of estimated Person
scores is not a substitute. Fixed-standard-normal MML uses a fixed SD of one;
it should not be described as estimating the standardizer. Conditional-normal
latent regression has a residual SD, which is a different estimand and is not
accepted by this population-SD transformation.

## Profile a difference with an estimated ability population

If the assessment model estimates an ability population rather than fixing it,
a small residual variance can make ordinary covariance-based intervals
unavailable. An explicit `method = "profile"` instead fixes the requested
difference in turn and reoptimizes the remaining parameters, including
nonnegative residual variance. Even when the center has zero residual variance,
the endpoints can have positive variance.

This experimental route accepts one named pairwise contrast for native direct
RSM/PCM MML, an estimated normal population, unit weights and unanchored centered
facets and steps. It excludes interactions, shrinkage, fixed population SD,
GPCM and standardized or simultaneous contrasts. The calculation can be
substantially slower than displaying a saved interval. Run the following code
explicitly; it is not evaluated during article construction.

```{r estimated-population-profile, eval=FALSE}
ratings <- load_mfrmr_data("example_core")
people <- unique(ratings["Person"])
fit <- fit_mfrm(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
  spec = list(model = "PCM", method = "MML", population_formula = ~1,
    person_data = people, person_id = "Person"))
facet_levels <- unique(as.character(ratings$Criterion))
contrast <- matrix(0, 1, length(facet_levels),
  dimnames = list("first_minus_second", facet_levels))
contrast[1, 1:2] <- c(1, -1)
ci <- mfrm_facet_intervals(fit, "Criterion", contrast, method = "profile")
summary(ci)
plot(ci)
results <- mfrm_results(fit, intervals = list(criterion = ci), compute = "never")
saveRDS(results, "profile-results.rds")
mfrm_report(readRDS("profile-results.rds"))
```

Read `SourceEstimate` and `ProfileEstimate` together. The source fit is retained
unchanged; the plotted `Estimate` uses the numerically checked profile center
when available. The table records its basis and likelihood improvement.
`SE` and the returned covariance are missing because this is not a Wald
interval. `profile` records evaluated differences, likelihood ratios and the
residual variance along the curve; numerical attempts and refused lower-order
calculations remain in `profile_attempts`. Missing bounds mean an unresolved
search, not zero uncertainty or proof of an infinite interval.

Check numerical integration separately from sample size. More ratings per
Person can concentrate that Person's likelihood enough to require finer
integration, even when the number of Persons is small. The native `method =
"model"` route can use a fit obtained with
`control = list(mml_engine = "direct", mml_integration = "adaptive")`,
within its documented scope. This changes the integration calculation, not
the assumed population distribution. The profile calculation also uses
Person-specific adaptive integration at positive residual variance, irrespective
of the source fit's integration setting. At zero variance it evaluates the
collapsed likelihood exactly, retaining the one-sided variance derivatives.
Adaptive integration shifts and scales the quadrature rule to the integrand;
see [Bilodeau, Stringer and Tang (2022, section 2.3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06801).
This numerical change does not alter the likelihood-ratio cutoff.
Inspect `numerical_checks` or `profile_attempts` and retain unavailable bounds
when verification fails. Increasing the grid alone need not resolve the
optimization. Numerical availability does not establish sampling coverage,
and a high descriptive reliability does not override an interval refusal.

The likelihood-ratio construction follows the definition discussed by
[Fischer and Lewis (2021, section 1.1)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-021-10012-y).
It uses a chi-square(1) reference approximation, whose applicability must be
distinguished from calculating the profile correctly. A nuisance parameter
on a boundary can change the reference distribution; see
[Self and Liang (1987, section 3)](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1987.10478472).
This implementation does not switch to a 50:50 mixture or select a cutoff
after inspecting the estimated variance.

A bounded saved study used a normal regression population, three fixed raters,
two fixed tasks and three categories. At 80 Persons with two ratings each and
residual variance 0.175, Task-difference interval availability increased from
158/199 to 199/199 for RSM and from 150/199 to 199/199 for PCM. Profile coverage
was 188/199 and 186/199, with exact Monte Carlo 95% intervals of 90.3--97.2%
and 89.1--96.5%. Coverage did not improve consistently on the inputs where
both procedures returned intervals. These are exploratory, condition-specific
results, not evidence that profile intervals always improve inference.
`CIEligible` describes numerical availability and `CoverageQualified` remains
`FALSE`; the method does not establish a minimum sample size or random-task
generalization. Its defaults leave the existing model-based method unchanged.

## Read fixed values and group constraints correctly

In the ordinary fixed-population RSM/PCM route, supplied anchors and group
means are treated as exact. Their source calibration error is not included.
`Status = "fixed"`, SE zero and missing bounds mean that the requested value
cannot vary under the declared constraints, rather than that it was estimated
with perfect precision.

This can happen even without a direct anchor for that level. With four raters
centered across the whole facet, fixing the first three raters' mean at 0.10
also fixes the fourth at -0.30. The first three can still differ; their
individual intervals may be available while an interval for their mean is not.
A difference between an anchored and a free rater can also remain uncertain.

The calculation carries the full joint covariance through the fitted
constraints and your comparison coefficients. It retains the uncertainty due
to estimating other facets and thresholds. Adding printed SEs, or calculating
information only for the selected rater, cannot replace that calculation.
For cross-software comparisons, note that
[TAM's `tam.se()` documentation](https://alexanderrobitzsch.github.io/TAM/reference/tam.se.html)
explicitly describes ignoring covariances between parameter estimates.
Match the uncertainty calculation as well as the response model.

Anchored models with an estimated population have a separate limitation:
their point estimates are supported, but the native location/population
interval helpers currently exclude anchors and group constraints. See the
[linking guide](https://ryuya-dot-com.github.io/mfrmr/dev/articles/mfrmr-linking-and-dff.html) for the distinction.

## Prepare a sheet for one rater

The functions below answer different practical questions. You can make a
figure or a report directly from saved results; neither is required before
saving the analysis.

| What do you need? | Function and returned object |
| --- | --- |
| Retain the fit, diagnostics and chosen intervals together | `mfrm_results()` returns the analysis object. |
| Show a saved interval | `plot()` draws it; `as_ggplot()` returns a supported ggplot view. |
| Read an analyst report | `mfrm_report()` returns a quality-control report by default. |
| Prepare one recipient's sheet | `mfrm_report(..., style = "rater", output = "html")` returns a temporary file path and its content. |
| Save the complete analysis for later work | `saveRDS()` writes one R object; `export_mfrm_results()` writes a folder of selected outputs. |

The development version can summarize one rater's saved results for a feedback
conversation. An individual interval and a difference between raters answer
different questions: attach `ordinary` here because it contains each rater's
coefficient. A saved contrast alone cannot become an individual interval.

```{r individual-sheet}
diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(fit, residual_pca = "none")
feedback_results <- mfrm_results(fit, diagnostics = diagnostics,
  intervals = list(raters = ordinary), compute = "never")
sheet <- mfrm_report(feedback_results, style = "rater", facet = "Rater",
  rater = "R01", interval = "raters", output = "html", max_cases = 5)
sheet$report$tables$severity
sheet$report$tables$uncertainty
# Open sheet$path in a browser. Review before copying the HTML file for sharing.
```

The file contains scoring tendency, its saved interval, exposure, ordinary
Infit/Outfit, category use and selected unexpected ratings. It has category-use
bars, numerical tables, print styling and no external resources. Set
`audience = "researcher"` for technical guidance, or `max_cases = 0` to omit
individual cases. Page count depends on the content and print settings.

Choose `style` for the report's purpose and `output` for its format. Omitting
`style` produces an analyst report, and omitting `output` returns an R object
without creating an HTML file. Neither `audience = "researcher"` nor
`output = "html"` selects a different interval method or confidence level:
those choices belong to the earlier `mfrm_facet_intervals()` call. The default
sheet includes up to five unexpected ratings; set `max_cases = 0` explicitly
if the conversation only needs aggregate summaries.

The default label is "Selected rater". Other raters' identities, Person
identifiers, task labels and original row numbers are omitted from the sheet
and its report object. An explicit `label` will be displayed. Scores or small
groups may still be recognizable, so review the content before sharing.
Distribute this standalone HTML file, not the comprehensive results bundle.

The sheet does not refit, recalculate uncertainty, select a warning threshold
or decide whether a rater is good or bad. Inspect the full saved interval
result and its numerical cautions before preparing the sheet. Missing inputs
are explained. If multiple attached interval results contain the selected
individual coefficient, choose one explicitly with `interval = "raters"`.
The supported contents depend on the fitted model:

| Fitted model | Individual sheet |
| --- | --- |
| Additive RSM/PCM, MML | Severity, supplied fixed-facet intervals, ordinary diagnostics and category use as illustrated here. |
| Additive RSM/PCM, ordinary JML | Descriptive severity, supplied diagnostics and category use; no formal fixed-facet interval is added. |
| Two-family GPCM, MML | Experimental location, component slope, category use and supplied posterior residuals. Only saved component-slope intervals appear in this sheet. |
| One-family GPCM, corrected JML, fitted interactions, imported fits, testlet or shared-random-rater models | Individual sheets are unavailable; use the model-specific analyst results and reports. |

For the two-family route, see the
[GPCM guide](https://ryuya-dot-com.github.io/mfrmr/dev/articles/mfrmr-gpcm-scope.html). Its locations, slopes and residuals have
different meanings from the ordinary-model quantities above. A successful
sheet export does not establish interval coverage or rater competence.

### Save the analysis and keep a copy of the sheet

The HTML path is temporary. To keep the sheet after the R session ends, copy
the reviewed file to a location you choose. Save the complete analysis
separately if you need to prepare another sheet later. The following example
uses temporary paths; replace them with your own analysis and recipient-file
paths for continuing work.

```{r feedback-save-reopen}
analysis_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(feedback_results, analysis_file)
saved_results <- readRDS(analysis_file)

# Reuse the saved diagnostics and intervals for this recipient.
saved_sheet <- mfrm_report(saved_results, style = "rater", facet = "Rater",
  rater = "R01", interval = "raters", output = "html", max_cases = 5)
recipient_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".html")
stopifnot(file.copy(saved_sheet$path, recipient_file, overwrite = FALSE))
```

The RDS file retains the fitted data and identifiers for the analyst. The
recipient HTML contains the selected summaries described above. Copying the
HTML does not require sending the RDS file. Reading the saved analysis and
preparing another sheet does not rerun estimation or diagnostics; it also
does not update an earlier analysis to reflect new ratings.

### Keep interpretation with exported tables

For a table-based handoff, request the recipient's tables rather than using
the full analyst export. Retain `interpretation_notes` alongside the numbers:
it explains the overall review status, the audience and each section, including
missing inputs. The HTML and Markdown formats already show these explanations
beside their sections.

```{r feedback-table-files}
sheet_tables <- mfrm_report(saved_results, style = "rater", facet = "Rater",
  rater = "R01", interval = "raters", output = "tables", max_cases = 5)
sheet_tables$interpretation_notes
table_dir <- tempfile("rater-tables-")
dir.create(table_dir)
for (name in names(sheet_tables)) {
  if (ncol(sheet_tables[[name]]) > 0) {
    write.csv(sheet_tables[[name]], file.path(table_dir, paste0(name, ".csv")),
      row.names = FALSE)
  }
}
```

Choose a permanent folder instead of `tempfile()` for continuing work.
Sections with no supplied table are explained in `interpretation_notes`;
their absence is not evidence of a satisfactory result. These CSV files do
not contain the fitted analysis and cannot be used to reconstruct it. Review
the selected rating examples before sharing, even though source identifiers
are omitted. Use `max_cases = 0` to exclude those examples.

## Carry the same intervals into figures and reports

Suppose the assessment team has chosen a rater difference and its interval
method. The figure, table and report should describe that same choice. Attach
the saved result instead of calculating a new interval during reporting:

```{r saved-intervals}
results <- mfrm_results(fit, intervals = list(difference = difference),
                        include = c("fit", "plots"), compute = "never")
apa_table(difference)
plot_data(results, type = "facet_difference", component = "table")
report <- mfrm_report(results)
report$tables$facet_difference_intervals
```

The name `difference` becomes the plot route `facet_difference`. A single
unnamed result, `intervals = difference`, uses `facet_inference`. Several
named results can retain different facets, confidence levels or prespecified
contrasts. They must all come from the same fitted analysis. A mismatch in
data, fitted parameters, constraints, population or integration settings is
rejected. An ordinary comparison interval remains separate from the selected
sandwich interval, including when the latter is unavailable.

```{r saved-interval-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.2, fig.alt="A saved rater-severity difference displayed with model-based and sandwich pointwise normal intervals. Vertical offsets and different line types distinguish the methods without relying only on color. The title and subtitle have been explicitly omitted."}
as_ggplot(results, type = "facet_difference", title = NULL, subtitle = NULL,
          preset = "monochrome")
```

Both `plot(results, type = "facet_difference")` and `as_ggplot(results, type = "facet_difference")`
return `ggplot` objects using the saved values. `title = NULL`, `subtitle = NULL`, `caption = NULL`,
`reference = NULL` and `show_legend = FALSE` omit the corresponding display
parts without changing the stored interval method, level or status. Keep
those details in the figure legend or accompanying text when publishing a
minimal figure. Shape cues retain unavailable and fixed targets.

`summary(results)$reproducible_code` shows how to save the complete result
and reload it later. In that code, `res` denotes your result object: use
`res <- results` for this example and choose the file path before saving.
Reloading preserves the attached intervals; reconstructing results from `fit`
alone would omit them.

`export_mfrm_results(results, ...)` includes the selected tables and figures.
With `preset = "starter"`, its `index.html` also links the saved interval
figures and describes their methods and confidence levels.
When replay is requested, it also saves the RDS and a script that reloads it;
replay does not refit the model or recalculate covariance. The settings,
contrast coefficients and cluster mapping are retained alongside the interval
table. These saved objects contain fitted data and participant identifiers;
follow the export function's data-handling guidance before sharing them.

For an analyst archive with tables, a report and reload instructions, select
the components explicitly. `include` controls files written by the exporter;
it does not compute missing analysis components. The folder below retains
participant data, which is why this example explicitly acknowledges it.

```{r interval-archive}
archive <- export_mfrm_results(feedback_results,
  output_dir = tempfile("rater-analysis-"),
  include = c("tables", "report", "replay", "manifest"),
  acknowledge_sensitive = TRUE)
# Count files by format; inspect archive$written_files for the full index.
table(archive$written_files$Format)
archive$plot_errors
saved_file <- archive$written_files$Path[
  archive$written_files$Component == "results_rds"]
reopened <- readRDS(saved_file)
stopifnot(identical(reopened$facet_intervals, feedback_results$facet_intervals))
```

Requesting replay also writes the complete RDS. The script reloads it without
requiring the original session's fit, diagnostics or interval variables.
No plots are requested in this example. Add `"plots"` to export available
figures, or use `preset = "starter"` for the fuller archive. This export
`preset` selects file contents; a plotting `preset` such as `"monochrome"`
selects appearance. An empty `plot_errors` table only confirms that no
requested plot failed, not that a figure was requested or that the statistical
analysis is valid. The report in this archive is the analyst report; use the
standalone recipient file created above for the feedback conversation.

This route also works for PCM, whose step structure is declared when fitting:

```{r pcm-saved-intervals}
fit_pcm <- fit_mfrm(ratings, "Person", c("Rater", "Criterion"), "Score",
                    model = "PCM", step_facet = "Criterion", method = "MML")
pcm_difference <- mfrm_facet_intervals(fit_pcm, "Rater", contrasts = contrast,
                                      method = "sandwich", level = 0.90)
pcm_results <- mfrm_results(fit_pcm, intervals = list(difference = pcm_difference),
                            include = c("fit", "plots"), compute = "never")
apa_table(pcm_difference)
```

RSM and PCM estimate facet locations while holding discrimination fixed;
GPCM slope intervals concern a different target. Attaching a fixed-facet
interval does not replace the uncertainty in an ordinary Wright map, alter
Infit/Outfit, or provide uncertainty for individual Person scores. Use the
`facet_` route when you want to display the attached covariance method.

## Declare what can be treated as independent

By default, all responses from one person form one sampling unit. A person
rated many times does not provide that many independent units. The software
first sums their likelihood contributions, then forms the sandwich covariance.
Repeated performances by the same person should not be treated as independent
merely because they were entered under different IDs.

If persons share a school, clinic or other source of dependence, and those
larger clusters can reasonably be treated as independent of one another, supply
a person-to-cluster mapping. This fictional mapping only demonstrates the syntax:
it is not evidence that the example contains actual schools.

```{r clusters}
persons <- sort(unique(ratings$Person))
schools <- data.frame(Person = persons,
  Cluster = rep(sprintf("School%02d", 1:16), each = 3))
school_difference <- mfrm_facet_intervals(
  fit, "Rater", contrasts = contrast, method = "sandwich", clusters = schools
)
school_difference$settings[c("persons", "clusters", "cluster_score_rank")]
summary(school_difference)
```

Every fitted person must appear exactly once. Use the column names `Person`
and `Cluster` in this mapping even if the original data use different names.
The number of independent clusters, rather than the number of rating rows,
governs the large-sample approximation. Sixteen schools in this illustration
are not a recommendation or a demonstrated sufficient sample size.

`adjust = TRUE` multiplies the covariance by `G/(G-1)`, where `G` is the number
of independent clusters. This simple scaling does not supply a small-sample
guarantee or change the normal reference distribution. It is off by default.
The user must justify the independence assumption; supplying a mapping does
not establish it.

## Keep unavailable results visible

When cluster likelihood scores do not span the free-parameter space, the
selected sandwich interval is unavailable. The estimate and ordinary comparison
remain visible. A fixed anchor has an exact supplied value and no inferential
interval; its uncertainty is outside this calculation.

```{r unavailable}
two_groups <- schools
two_groups$Cluster <- rep(c("A", "B"), each = 24)
unavailable <- mfrm_facet_intervals(
  fit, "Rater", contrasts = contrast, method = "sandwich", clusters = two_groups
)
summary(unavailable)[, c("Target", "Estimate", "Lower", "Upper", "Status")]
```

Increasing the cluster count until this numerical restriction disappears does
not establish coverage. A small number of clusters can still yield poor
intervals. In plots, a cross marks an unavailable selected interval and an open
diamond marks a fixed target. An ordinary comparison interval is never used to
replace a missing sandwich interval.

## Understand what the sandwich can and cannot address

With many independent units and the required regularity, a sandwich covariance
describes variation around the parameter targeted by the fitted working model.
If that model is misspecified, this *pseudo-true parameter* can differ from the
generating rater severity. For example, a strongly skewed ability distribution
can change the limiting rater difference when the fit insists on a standard
normal distribution. Altering the standard error does not remove that shift.

Sparse assignment also needs substantive review. An unassigned rating is not
a missing score to fill in; selective assignment can confound rater differences
with population differences. Nonresponse depending on an unobserved score is
another modeling problem. None of these problems is solved solely by selecting
`method = "sandwich"`.

The intervals condition on the observed **fixed** raters and other facets.
They do not describe replacing raters with new draws from a rater population.
If shared random rater or task effects span the declared clusters, this one-way
independence assumption is inappropriate. The method is not a multiway
crossed-cluster estimator. G/D-study planning, variance-component boundaries,
EAP person-score uncertainty and multiple-imputation pooling require their own
methods. In particular, `pool_mfrm_imputed()` continues to use its documented
within-imputation model covariance; this helper does not change that workflow.

For model and sandwich intervals, review quadrature sensitivity separately:
these methods reuse the fitted integration grid without refitting. The profile
method described above reoptimizes nuisance parameters and checks integration
throughout the profile.

## What the bounded simulation showed

A comparison used RSM and PCM, 80 or 320 independent persons, three fixed
raters, two criteria and scores from 0 to 2. Each of the eight conditions had
200 independently generated datasets. One scenario used standard-normal
ability and six ratings per person. The other combined standardized lognormal
ability with three ratings per person; assignment was independent of ability
and responses. Thus the second scenario challenges both distribution and
design together, without isolating their separate effects.

The comparison evaluated three rater differences and one criterion difference
on each same fitted dataset. All 1,600 datasets returned both interval methods.
The entries below are **ranges across conditions and contrasts**, not pooled
coverage estimates or confidence bounds. All intervals had a nominal 95% level.

| Scenario and reference target | Observed information | Sandwich |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Matched normal model: generating truth | 92.0–98.0% | 92.5–98.0% |
| Skewed ability and sparse assignment: generating truth | 84.5–95.0% | 87.0–95.5% |
| Skewed ability and sparse assignment: working-model target | 90.0–97.5% | 93.0–97.5% |

For example, in the 320-person RSM scenario with skewed ability and sparse
assignment, the sandwich covered the generating criterion difference in
87.0% of datasets (95% Monte Carlo interval: 81.5–91.3%). Coverage of the
independently calculated working-model target was 96.0% (92.3–98.3%). The
same estimates and intervals produced these different answers because the
two target values differ. For the R1–R3 difference in the corresponding
320-person PCM scenario, generating-truth coverage was 90.0% (85.0–93.8%).
Rater comparisons are therefore subject to this limitation too.

With 200 datasets per condition, Monte Carlo standard error near 95% coverage
is about 1.54 percentage points. These results do not demonstrate uniform
improvement or a guarantee of nominal coverage. Schools, few independent
clusters, shared random raters, informative assignment and nonresponse were
not evaluated by this simulation.

## Sample-size stability

**Plan for a target and an acceptable error, then choose the number of people
and their rating assignments.** A count by itself cannot establish stability.
The guidance below defines what to assess and gives a bounded worked example;
it does not yet establish recommended minimum sizes for classroom designs.

### State what needs to be stable

| Intended use | Target to assess | Design information to retain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discuss a difference between two raters | Their severity contrast, with its covariance | Distinct persons per rater, shared performances, categories and assignment pattern |
| Score an individual | Ability or a specified expected score | That person's tasks and raters, targeting, and whether calibration uncertainty is included |
| Compare cohorts or link years | A cohort contrast on a declared common scale | Persons per cohort, common recordings, anchor uncertainty and drift assumptions |
| Plan future assessments | A specified G/Phi or observed-score precision target | Random versus fixed facets, task/rater pools and the intended generalization universe |

Keep **Persons, performances, tasks, criteria, rater pool size, raters per
performance and score rows** separate. Twenty writers producing two essays
are twenty writers with repeated performances. Seven criteria do not become
seven independent tasks. `facet_small_sample_review()` describes retained
rating counts and distinct recorded Person IDs. Its default 10/30/50 count
bands are screening choices, not sample-size recommendations or precision
qualifications.

Use the following dimensions together:

1. **Numerical availability:** identify which points and intervals the method
   can provide, and why others are unavailable. A finite number or optimizer
   convergence is not evidence of small sampling error.
2. **Point accuracy:** assess bias, RMSE and the proportion of estimates within
   a prespecified error of the generating target. Relative bias is unsuitable
   when the target is zero or near zero. In empirical data the truth is unknown;
   sensitivity checks do not directly measure this error.
3. **Interval precision and calibration:** assess both interval width and
   coverage. A narrow interval can miss too often; a very wide interval can
   cover well while providing little practical precision.
4. **Sensitivity:** examine plausible ability distributions, severity spreads,
   rare categories, incomplete assignments and dependence between ratings.
   Larger samples do not repair confounding or a misspecified response model.

For a two-sided interval, define its radius around the reported estimate as
`max(Estimate - Lower, Upper - Estimate)`. This also handles asymmetric
intervals. A legitimate one-sided or unbounded interval can be available
while failing a finite-radius target; distinguish it from an unresolved
numerical calculation. Preserve all attempted datasets in the availability
and precision denominators. Also report coverage among available intervals
and the proportion of all attempts that both provide an interval and cover.

Choose acceptable error and radius in relation to the decision, before
evaluating a proposed design. For example, a team could examine a 0.5-logit
radius for a severity difference and ask for an available interval this
narrow in at least 90% of repeated samples. **Both numbers are illustrative
planning choices, not validated mfrmr defaults.** Translate the contrast to
expected-score differences for a stated rubric and ability range when that
makes the consequence easier to judge. Separate the desired precision of a
point estimate from the desired width of its confidence interval.

### What existing evidence can tell us

[Linacre's Rasch guidance](https://www.rasch.org/rmt/rmt74m.htm) relates
precision to targeting and SE: its approximate 95% examples use 16–36
respondents for item calibration within 1 logit, and 64–144 within 0.5 logits.
These are not guarantees for a many-facet contrast, a discrimination
parameter, or arbitrary partial-credit category use. Counting every criterion
rating as another independent respondent would misapply the guidance.
[Schroeders and Gnambs (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1177/25152459251314798)
instead show how IRT sample planning can be tailored to the target, response
model and assignment/missingness design. This is the approach used here.

An earlier RSM/PCM study illustrates why the target and assignment matter.
The following is an **exploratory reanalysis of saved results**, with the
0.5-logit radius selected for illustration after that study. It is not an
independent confirmation of a sample-size recommendation.

<details>
<summary>View the design-specific results and their limits</summary>

Each model/design had 200 simulated datasets. The target was the fixed
R1-minus-R2 severity contrast, truly 0.4 logits. Ratings used categories 0–2;
the RSM shared steps and the PCM used task-specific steps. Direct MML
estimated a correctly specified normal ability regression with true mean
`0.2 + 0.5 * X` and residual variance 0.7. Raters and tasks were fixed effects,
and ratings were conditionally independent. The intervals below are ordinary
joint-information Wald intervals, not the newer profile intervals.

"Narrow" means available with radius at most 0.5 logits, divided by **all
200 attempts**. Coverage counts use the separately stated available denominator.

| Persons | Rater pool | Task pool | Ratings/person | Narrow, RSM / PCM | Covered/available, RSM / PCM |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- | --- |
| 80 | 3 | 2 | 6 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 190/200 / 189/200 |
| 240 | 3 | 2 | 6 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 190/200 / 195/200 |
| 80 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 0/200 / 0/200 | 195/198 / 182/195 |
| 240 | 3 | 2 | 2 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 187/200 / 192/200 |
| 80 | 6 | 2 | 6 | 94/200 / 117/200 | 191/200 / 190/200 |
| 80 | 3 | 4 | 6 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 188/200 / 189/200 |
| 80 | 6 | 2 | 12 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 192/200 / 191/200 |
| 80 | 3 | 4 | 12 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 191/200 / 191/200 |
| 160 | 3 | 2 | 6 | 200/200 / 200/200 | 183/200 / 190/200 |

The six-rating, three-rater design crosses all raters and tasks. The
two-rating design assigns one rater to each task in a connected cyclic
pattern. At six ratings per person, the six-rater design assigns three raters
to both tasks, and the four-task design assigns all three raters to two tasks.
The twelve-rating designs are fully crossed.

For 80 persons, moving from six to two ratings reduced the number of narrow
intervals from 200 to zero in both models. Holding persons and total ratings
fixed while expanding the rater pool from three to six reduced the narrow
fraction to 47.0% for RSM and 58.5% for PCM. Their pointwise 95% Monte Carlo
intervals are 39.9–54.2% and 51.3–65.4%. These are simulation-uncertainty
intervals, not intervals for the severity contrast.

Even perfect observed width attainment does not qualify coverage. For example,
the 160-person RSM condition produced 200 narrow intervals but covered in
183/200 datasets: 91.5%, with a 95% Monte Carlo interval of 86.7–95.0%
(upper endpoint before rounding: 94.9704%). The result is retained alongside
the more favorable conditions. There is no monotonic coverage guarantee as
person count increases.

Point accuracy answers another question. In the 80-person, two-rating design,
finite estimates were within 0.5 logits of truth in 181/200 RSM datasets and
170/200 PCM datasets, although no interval met the 0.5-logit radius target.
Finite points include cases with unavailable covariance; this count does not
requalify their uncertainty or prove numerical admissibility.

The counts can be used to reproduce the reported Monte Carlo limits:

```{r sample-guidance-mc, eval=FALSE}
binom.test(94, 200)$conf.int   # RSM: available and narrow
binom.test(117, 200)$conf.int  # PCM: available and narrow
binom.test(183, 200)$conf.int  # RSM: coverage in the 160-person design
```

This recalculates uncertainty from reported counts; it does not reproduce
the underlying fits. Each comparison concerns one prespecified contrast,
not simultaneous accuracy of every rater. These results do not establish
Person-score coverage, random-rater generalization, or adequacy for a
20–40-person classroom with seven correlated criteria. Equal score-row
counts also need not imply equal total assessment costs.

</details>

### More facets, fit screening and reliability

Adding a facet, increasing its number of levels, and adding an interaction
change different parts of an assessment. Report all three separately. The
number of facet types alone is not a multiplier for the required sample size.
Also distinguish adding model parameters to existing ratings from collecting
additional tasks or rating occasions.

<details>
<summary>How these choices extend the sample-size guide</summary>

**Facet structure.** Consider 32 writers, each producing two essays, four
raters with two assigned to each essay, and seven criteria: 896 score rows.
Counterbalance the two tasks across two occasions to separate their effects.
The following are algebraic counts for ordinary additive models with four
categories, centered non-Person locations and steps, and an estimated normal
population mean and variance. PCM steps belong to Criterion. Person ability
is integrated out, so these MML counts do not include 32 individual abilities.

| Model facets, including Person | Free RSM parameters | Free PCM parameters |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Person, Rater, Criterion | 13 | 25 |
| Add two-level Task | 14 | 26 |
| Also add two-level Occasion | 15 | 27 |
| Same five facets, plus Rater × Criterion interaction | 33 | 45 |

These are parameter counts, not minimum sample sizes or fitted performance.
Omitting a task or occasion with a nonzero effect can bias the simpler model;
fewer parameters alone do not make it preferable. With four raters and seven
criteria, the interaction adds `(4 - 1) * (7 - 1) = 18` contrasts, although
the number of facet types stays five. Conversely, increasing Criterion from
seven to fourteen levels changes a facet's size rather than creating seven
new facets. Counts for fixed-population MML, JML, CML or slope models differ.

If Task 1 is always on Occasion 1 and Task 2 always on Occasion 2, their main
effects are confounded. The synthetic assignment's conditional additive
design has rank 42 rather than 43; counterbalancing gives rank 43. Adding
writers with the same confounding cannot fix this. Full rank itself does not
prove marginal identification, finite-MLE existence or adequate precision.
Likewise, a training-group effect cannot be separated from unrestricted
individual-rater effects when each rater belongs to exactly one group without
additional constraints or a different hierarchical estimand.

**Infit and Outfit.** These assess residual patterns relative to a model;
they do not directly measure the precision of a severity estimate. Infit
weights squared standardized residuals by response information. Outfit is
more affected by unexpected responses where model variance is small. Means
near one are reference values, not proof that a sample is adequate. The
distribution after fitting parameters must be distinguished from a calculation
at known parameters.

[Smith et al. (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1186/1471-2288-8-33) found relatively
stable average mean squares but strongly sample-sensitive standardized
statistics in resampled polytomous questionnaire data. This does not establish
universal false-flag rates. [Müller (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40488-020-00108-7)
shows that residual construction, sample size and test length affect the
distribution in dichotomous Rasch models. Neither result directly calibrates
all many-facet MML diagnostics.

For a diagnostic recommendation, evaluate:

- False flags for each unaffected rater and the probability of at least one
  false flag across the declared comparison family.
- Detection of specified departures, such as Person × Rater dependence,
  inappropriate category use or a response pattern outside the fitted model.
- Missing diagnostics, category support and the effect of any selection,
  exclusion or refitting included in the actual procedure.

A constant severity difference is not itself misfit. A slope difference that
violates RSM can be part of a specified GPCM; detection targets must name the
model. A fixed 0.7–1.3 MnSq band or `abs(ZSTD) > 2` is not automatically a
calibrated test at every sample size. Freeze the residual basis, estimation
method, degrees-of-freedom convention and transformation before comparison.
[Guo and Wind (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1177/01466216211013105) investigate
parametric-bootstrap alternatives specifically for rater fit; this makes
design-specific calibration a candidate, not a blanket justification for
automatic rater removal or for transferring their cutoffs to another model.

The existing `mfrm_screening_performance()` accepts planned simulation targets
and observed flags and keeps unavailable outcomes and family-level events.
It can summarize the required operating characteristics without treating
correlated raters as independent simulation replications. It does not generate
calibrated flags. `evaluate_mfrm_diagnostic_screening()` supplies exploratory
scenario comparisons, not already-established inferential power.

**Reliability.** Name the coefficient and its intended population before
setting a target such as 0.8 or 0.9.

| Quantity | Interpretation and sample-size concern |
| --- | --- |
| Person separation reliability | Distinguishability relative to the spread of estimated abilities; a restricted ability range can lower it even with the same absolute SE |
| Rater separation reliability | Distinguishability of severities; a high value does not mean high agreement, and a low value can reflect imprecision |
| Inter-rater agreement | Agreement of scores under a declared design; it is not a separation coefficient |
| Posterior-variance EAP reliability | A distinct population/scoring quantity; do not substitute the separation formula applied to EAP estimates |
| G/Phi | Observed-score generalization under a declared G-Study/D-Study design; task/rater universes and relative/absolute decisions matter |

The separation/agreement distinction is also explicit in the
[FACETS manual](https://www.winsteps.com/facetman64/reliability.htm).
For ordinary mfrmr diagnostics, the separation index is
`max(s^2 - mean(SE^2), 0) / s^2`, where `s^2` is the sample variance of the
included finite estimates and every included level must have a valid SE.
Zero observed variance, incomplete uncertainty or fixed anchors can make the
index unavailable. This approximate calculation does not propagate covariance
among estimates and does not supply a formal confidence interval.

An algebraic illustration, checked against the calculation used by the package,
holds the RMS SE at 0.30 and varies the **observed estimate SD**:

| Observed estimate SD | RMS SE | Separation reliability |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 0.40 | 0.30 | 0.4375 |
| 0.80 | 0.30 | 0.8594 |
| 1.20 | 0.30 | 0.9375 |

These are not simulation results or different sample sizes. They show why a
higher coefficient cannot, by itself, establish better absolute precision.
Do not select a broader sample merely to raise reliability. In a performance
study, retain the intended ability range and report score RMSE/SE and relevant
classification errors alongside the coefficient and its sampling variation.
For only four or eight raters, also distinguish a descriptive spread of those
fixed raters from inference about a population of future raters.

mfrmr's fit-adjusted `RealSE` multiplies `ModelSE` by
`sqrt(max(Infit, 1))`. Its corresponding reliability and the model index are
companion summaries, not confidence limits or independent corroboration of
fit. Person rows using EAP and posterior SD retain the separation-index
limitation. Ordinary reliability plotting does not support corrected JML or
two-family GPCM. Inspect the applicable method rather than borrowing another
model's coefficient.

For a supported ordinary fit, the existing workflow is:

```{r sample-guidance-diagnostics, eval=FALSE}
diagnostics <- diagnose_mfrm(fit, diagnostic_mode = "both", residual_pca = "none")
diagnostics$measures
diagnostics$reliability
reliability_plot <- plot(fit, type = "reliability", draw = FALSE)
plot_data(reliability_plot, "table")
plot_data(reliability_plot, "notes")
```

The next classroom evaluations can reuse the same simulated data and eligible
fits for precision, screening and reliability summaries. Their success criteria
remain distinct. Existing severity-interval coverage results do not establish
Infit false-flag rates or reliability-interval coverage.

</details>

### How a recommendation will be qualified

For anchors and bias/DFF, the required resources differ again: distinguish
the source-calibration sample, independent linking performances, the receiving
sample, and independent Persons within each target cell or group. Conditional
precision with fixed anchors, propagation of estimated-anchor error, and
sensitivity to anchor drift answer different questions. Likewise, a
fixed-calibration bias screen is not a jointly estimated interaction interval.
Use the [linking and DFF guide](mfrmr-linking-and-dff.html#which-uncertainty-is-available-with-anchors)
to select the supported route before applying the planning criteria below.

A useful recommendation states the model and estimator, target and scale,
assignment, precision goal, evaluated sensitivity range, and Monte Carlo
uncertainty. It should distinguish **evidence supporting the declared goal**,
**evidence that the goal is not met**, **inconclusive evidence**, and
**conditions outside the evaluated scope**. These are interpretations of a
study, not new fit-status fields or count-based rejection rules.

In particular, observing approximately 95% coverage is insufficient to
establish calibration. Declare a tolerance around the nominal level and
check whether the Monte Carlo interval lies within it; overlapping a boundary
can leave the conclusion unresolved. Similarly, a precision-attainment rate
near its required minimum needs its Monte Carlo uncertainty. With 200
replications, the approximate 95% Monte Carlo half-width near 95% coverage is
3 percentage points. About 2,000 *available* replications reduce it to roughly
1 point, but other rates, multiple targets and unavailable intervals can
require more. Follow the performance-measure and simulation-precision
principles in [Morris, White and Crowther (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086).

The classroom extension starts with the published example of 32 writers,
four raters, two raters per essay and seven criteria in
[Nakamura (2002)](https://pansig.org/publications/pansig/2002/HTML/Nakamura.htm).
Comparisons vary writers, ratings per essay and rater pool separately, retain
a larger-sample reference, and examine dependence and category support.
Selecting a promising design in exploratory results and independently
confirming its performance are separate steps. Until that evidence exists,
32 persons is a realistic study scenario, not a recommended minimum.

## Save the analysis and use the plotted data

```{r save}
saved <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(difference, saved)
restored <- readRDS(saved)
summary(restored)
plotted <- plot(restored, draw = FALSE)
plot_data(plotted)$table
```

The saved result retains the estimates, covariance matrices, likelihood scores,
cluster mapping, contrasts, settings and source fit. Printing or plotting it
does not fit the model again. Use `write.csv(result$table, "intervals.csv",
row.names = FALSE)` to export a table, and keep the RDS result for its context.
Both `plot()` and `as_ggplot()` return `ggplot` objects for these method
comparisons, and `plot_data()` extracts the underlying tables for custom graphics.

## References

The sandwich construction follows the estimating-function framework described
by [Zeileis (2006)](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v016.i09).
[Zeileis, Koell and Graham (2020)](https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v095.i01)
discuss clustered covariance estimators and their distinctions. These references
support the covariance framework; they do not establish finite-sample accuracy
for every MFRM design.
